title: Choosing a WinSCP Alternative: Start With the Job, Not the App
summary:
WinSCP already does a lot: SFTP, SCP, FTP/FTPS, WebDAV and S3, plus directory synchronization and Windows scripting. If you’re looking for an alternative, the useful question isn’t “Which app is best?” It’s “Which part of my workflow does WinSCP no longer fit?”

That distinction matters. A tool that works on macOS may not offer WinSCP’s automation, and an SSH terminal with a file browser may not replace a dedicated transfer client.

First, identify the task you need to replace

List what you actually use before comparing apps:

  • Moving files manually: Do you need a two-pane browser, transfer queue, or support for several protocols?
  • Connecting from another operating system: Are you moving to macOS or Linux, where WinSCP doesn’t offer a native desktop app?
  • Working with cloud storage: Do you need S3, Google Drive, OneDrive, or another provider?
  • Administering a server: Do you want a terminal and file browser together, or are you happy using separate tools?
  • Automating transfers: Do existing scripts, scheduled jobs, or .NET integrations depend on WinSCP?
  • Mounting remote files: Do you want remote storage to appear in Finder or File Explorer, rather than opening a transfer client?

These are different needs. A mount tool, a terminal emulator, and an SFTP client aren’t interchangeable just because each can access remote files.

It also helps to check the protocol requirement. SFTP runs over SSH; FTPS is FTP secured with TLS. They’re distinct protocols, so a client supporting one doesn’t necessarily support the other. If you’re weighing transfer options, this SFTP client comparison can help you narrow the category before picking an app.

Shortlist by operating system and workflow

If you want a free, cross-platform file-transfer client

FileZilla Client is a straightforward starting point for FTP, FTPS, and SFTP on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Its standard client is free. Some cloud integrations are part of FileZilla Pro, so check which edition supports the services you need.

It’s a practical choice when your core job is browsing local and remote files and transferring them. It isn’t a one-for-one substitute for WinSCP’s Windows scripting and .NET assembly.

If you need SFTP plus cloud storage

Cyberduck is available for Windows and macOS and supports SFTP alongside a range of cloud storage services. The base app is free and open source. It’s a file and storage browser, not an interactive SSH terminal, and it doesn’t have a native Linux desktop release.

If you’re on macOS

ForkLift offers a Mac-native, two-pane file-manager workflow with remote connections and cloud services. Transmit is another paid Mac option focused on transfers and synchronization. They’re not Linux or Windows replacements, and their licensing differs. Check current platform requirements and terms before buying.

If you want a Windows SSH terminal and graphical SFTP

Bitvise SSH Client combines SSH terminal and graphical SFTP workflows on Windows. It’s a reasonable option if you’ve been using WinSCP alongside a separate terminal client.

MobaXterm is a broader Windows toolbox that includes SSH, SFTP, and tools for other remote-access workflows such as X11. Its free Home edition has limits; check the current edition details if saved sessions, tunnels, or macros matter to you.

If automation is the priority

Don’t switch away from WinSCP just because a different client has a newer interface. WinSCP’s scripting interface and .NET assembly can be important parts of a deployment or backup process. A graphical alternative may not run those jobs, and another command-line tool won’t automatically understand existing WinSCP scripts.

For cross-platform transfer automation, rclone is worth evaluating. It supports SFTP and many cloud backends, but it’s a command-line tool rather than a two-pane file manager. Be especially careful with synchronization: rclone sync can delete files at the destination to make it match the source. Test paths and use a dry run before relying on a new job.

Also distinguish SCP from SFTP when migrating. WinSCP supports both, but many modern workflows use SFTP; this explanation of how SCP and SFTP differ is useful if an old script or server specifically requires SCP.

Migrate without breaking a working setup

Treat a client migration like a small infrastructure change—not just an app install.

  1. Inventory your saved sites. Record hostnames, ports, usernames, protocols, key locations, proxy or jump-host settings, and default remote directories.
  2. Find every automation dependency. Search for scheduled tasks, scripts, and applications that invoke WinSCP. A site you rarely open manually may still be used by a nightly job.
  3. Recreate connections using supported import tools. Don’t assume a destination client can import WinSCP’s settings. An export file can also contain sensitive connection details, so protect it accordingly.
  4. Verify the server’s identity. When the new client first connects, check the host-key fingerprint through a trusted channel. Don’t accept a changed or unfamiliar key just to get past a warning.
  5. Test a harmless transfer. Confirm the remote directory, permissions, file contents, and transfer direction before editing production files or changing a sync job.
  6. Keep a rollback path. Retain the old configuration and scripts until the replacement has passed the real tasks you depend on.

A practical decision rule

If you use Windows and mainly need reliable file transfers or mature WinSCP scripts, staying with WinSCP may be the simplest choice. If you need a native Mac or Linux client, start with a cross-platform transfer tool. If you want a Windows terminal alongside graphical SFTP, evaluate an SSH client that includes both. If repeatable automation is the job, test the replacement’s command-line behavior before migrating production tasks.

The best alternative is the one that covers the specific gap without quietly removing a feature you rely on. If WinSCP still handles your workflow, there’s no technical prize for replacing it.

I originally published a more detailed version of this guide on the SSHFlow blog.

I'm also building SSHFlow — an SSH client where every server gets its own workspace for terminals, SFTP, code, and databases.

title: 1Z0-078 Lists RAC First, but Your Cluster Is Built from the Bottom Up
summary:
If you run Oracle databases on more than one server, you already know the order things happen in on a real cluster. Someone prepares the operating system, the shared disks and the networks. Then Grid Infrastructure goes on, which brings Oracle Clusterware and Oracle Automatic Storage Management with it. Only after that does anyone install the database software, and only after that does a RAC database exist to tune, patch and connect to.

Oracle's exam page for 1Z0-078 lists the same material in the opposite order. It starts with RAC databases and architecture, moves on to Grid Infrastructure in the middle, and ends with ASM disk groups, files and the ASM Cluster File System. That is a fine way to describe a job. It is a poor way to learn one, because almost every RAC objective assumes you understand the layers underneath it.

This article follows the build order instead. It is written for the DBA or systems administrator who already looks after clustered databases and wants to know whether 1Z0-078 matches the work on their desk. Every number in it comes from Oracle's own exam page and Oracle's 19c documentation, both checked on 15 October 2026.

What Is the Oracle 1Z0-078 RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Exam?

1Z0-078 is the exam behind the Oracle Certified Professional, Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administrator credential. Its full title on Oracle MyLearn is "Exam 1Z0-078: Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administration", and the official 1Z0-078 exam page on Oracle MyLearn is where the topic list, the format and the session rules live.

Oracle describes the audience plainly. The certification is for database production systems administrators and database administrators with 12 to 18 months of experience using RAC, ASM and Grid Infrastructure. The exam measures installation, configuration, backup and recovery, monitoring and tuning of those components. Read that as a description of who does well, not as an entry rule: the page states an experience profile, and it is worth being honest with yourself about whether you match it.

The three names in the title are three layers of one stack, and it helps to be precise about how they relate, because the exam is.

Grid Infrastructure: the base layer

Oracle's Introduction to Oracle Clusterware in the 19c Clusterware Administration and Deployment Guide explains that Clusterware lets separate servers communicate so they appear to applications and users as one system. Since Oracle Clusterware 12c, the Clusterware and ASM binaries are installed as a single binary called Oracle Grid Infrastructure. The same guide notes that Clusterware 19c supports only ASM 19c, because ASM sits in the Grid Infrastructure home that also holds Clusterware.

Clusterware keeps two stored components besides its binaries. Voting files record node membership. The Oracle Cluster Registry, or OCR, records cluster configuration: databases, listeners, virtual IP addresses, services and any applications Clusterware manages. Both must sit on shared storage that every cluster node can reach.

ASM: the storage layer

ASM is Oracle's volume manager and file system for database files. Oracle's overview chapter of the 19c ASM Administrator's Guide describes disk groups made of disks, files and allocation units, with normal redundancy giving two-way mirroring, high redundancy three-way mirroring, and external redundancy leaving the mirroring to a RAID subsystem.

RAC: the database layer

Oracle RAC lets several instances open one database. The RAC guide says that having multiple instances access a single database prevents the server from being a single point of failure, and that applications deployed on RAC databases can operate without code changes. RAC depends on Clusterware; the guide calls Clusterware a required component that provides the infrastructure RAC runs on.

So the order on the exam page is top-down, while the order on a real system is bottom-up. Hold on to that idea. It shapes the study plan later in this article.

1Z0-078 Exam Overview and Details

The format is short to state. Everything below is from Oracle's exam page unless marked otherwise.

  • Exam code: 1Z0-078
  • Exam name: Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administration
  • Credential: Oracle Certified Professional, Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administrator
  • Delivery: Proctored Online
  • Format: Multiple Choice
  • Duration: 120 minutes
  • Number of questions: 77
  • Passing score: 65%
  • Price: Oracle's page shows no price to a signed-out visitor. The DBExam syllabus page lists USD $245 and notes that pricing may vary by country or local currency; confirm the figure in your Oracle account at checkout.

What 77 questions in 120 minutes means at the desk

120 minutes across 77 questions is about 93 seconds a question. That is generous for a question that asks you to recognise a view name and tight for one that describes a failed node, a set of services and a client configuration, then asks what the client sees. Plan to move quickly through recall questions so the scenario questions get the time they need.

A 65% passing score on 77 questions works out to just over 50 correct answers, if every question counts the same. Oracle does not publish how it weights individual questions, so treat 51 as a planning number rather than a rule, and aim well above it.

Session rules worth knowing in advance

  • A government-issued identification is required to take the exam.
  • Check-in time is 30 minutes before the exam time.
  • Your computer must meet Oracle's minimum system requirements for online proctoring.
  • Results are shown on screen at the close of the exam, and the detailed score report is in Oracle CertView.
  • To reschedule, you must do it at least 24 hours before your appointment time.

None of these is unusual, but the 30-minute check-in catches people who block exactly two hours in their calendar. Block three.

Key Topics and Syllabus for 1Z0-078

Oracle's exam page lists 30 topics and 115 objective lines under three groupings. The first grouping has no heading of its own on the page; it is the RAC material. Then come the headings "Grid Infrastructure Administration" and "Automatic Storage Management (ASM) Administration". Counted line by line:

  • RAC administration: 12 topics, 49 objective lines
  • Grid Infrastructure administration: 11 topics, 41 objective lines
  • ASM administration: 7 topics, 25 objective lines

One caution before you use those counts: Oracle publishes no percentage weights for 1Z0-078. A line count shows where the page spends its words, not how many questions each area gets. The 1Z0-078 syllabus on DBExam sets the same topics out on one page with the exam facts beside them, which is handy as a checklist.

Here is the syllabus in the order you would build the system, bottom layer first.

Layer 1: Grid Infrastructure and Clusterware (11 topics)

The Grid Infrastructure grouping covers the life of the cluster itself:

  • Introduction to Clusterware and Oracle Clusterware architecture, including startup details and how Grid Plug and Play affects Clusterware
  • Flex Clusters and the effect of node failure in one
  • Installation planning and pre-tasks: system and network requirements, groups, users and directories
  • Grid Infrastructure installation, verifying it, configuring ASM disk groups, and the optional Grid Infrastructure Management Repository
  • Managing cluster nodes: extending a cluster, deleting a node, and adding nodes with DBCA
  • Traditional Clusterware management: day-to-day tasks, OCR backup and recovery, network settings, what-if command evaluation and secure cluster communication
  • Policy-based cluster management: server categorization, policy sets and activating a policy
  • Upgrading and patching Grid Infrastructure, including rolling patches and zero-downtime Grid Infrastructure patching
  • Troubleshooting Clusterware: log files, diagcollection.pl, resource and component debugging, and OCR problems
  • Making applications highly available with Clusterware: policy-managed and administrator-managed databases, application VIPs and application resources

Two documented facts from this layer tend to matter. First, Oracle recommends no more than five voting files, although Clusterware supports up to 15. Second, you can have up to five OCR locations, and you can replace a failed OCR location online as long as it is not the only one. Small numbers like these make good exam distractors, so learn them exactly.

Flex Clusters have their own rules in the Clusterware Administration and Deployment Guide: a Flex Cluster can have as many as 64 Hub Nodes, Hub Nodes have direct access to shared storage and host read-write instances, other nodes request data through Hub Nodes and host read-only instances, Flex Clusters require Grid Naming Service, and you can convert a standard cluster to a Flex Cluster but not the reverse.

Layer 2: ASM, ACFS and ADVM (7 topics)

The ASM grouping is the shortest, but it sits under everything else:

  • ASM architecture and components
  • ASM instances: initialization parameters, processes, and monitoring with the V$ASM dynamic performance views
  • Flex ASM: architecture, installation, configuration and management
  • Disk groups: creating, dropping, setting attributes, maintenance, and performance and scalability considerations
  • Files, directories and templates, including the format of a fully qualified ASM file name
  • Oracle CloudFS: the ASM Dynamic Volume Manager, ASM volumes, ACFS and ACFS snapshots
  • CloudFS advanced topics: ACFS auditing, encryption, replication and tagging, and High Availability NFS

The file name objective is a good example of how literal the exam can be. Oracle's chapter on ASM files, directories and templates gives the form as +diskgroup/dbname/filetype/filetypetag.file.incarnation in a non-multitenant database, and +diskgroup/cdb/pdb_guid/filetype/filetypetag.file.incarnation with multitenant. Alias names are told apart because they do not end in a dotted pair of numbers. If you can read +DATA/ORCL/DATAFILE/system.257.967544915 and name every field, that objective is done.

Flex ASM gets three objective lines. The key documented behaviour is in Oracle's Managing Oracle Flex ASM chapter: a small set of ASM instances serves the whole cluster, the number is set with a cardinality setting, and the default is three instances. The ASM overview adds why it matters: in a standard ASM cluster, if the ASM instance on a node fails, the database instances on that node fail too, while with Flex ASM a database instance can reach another ASM instance on another node.

Layer 3: The RAC database (12 topics)

RAC gets the most objective lines, and it is where most candidates already feel at home:

  • RAC architecture: the benefits of RAC, why global resources are needed, and global cache coordination
  • Installing and configuring RAC, creating a cluster database, and converting a single-instance database to RAC
  • Administering RAC: redo log files, undo tablespaces, starting and stopping, and initialization parameters
  • Backup and recovery: ARCHIVELOG mode, the fast recovery area, and RMAN in a RAC environment
  • Global resources: the Global Resource Directory, global enqueue and instance locks, global buffer cache management, and affinity
  • Monitoring and tuning: RAC wait events, AWR and ADDM in RAC, the Cluster Database Performance pages, and SGA runtime management
  • High availability of services, and high availability for connections and applications: load balancing, the Load Balancing Advisory, FAN, TAF, Transparent Application Continuity and Dynamic Services Fallback
  • Upgrading and patching RAC with OUI and opatch
  • RAC One Node conversions in both directions
  • Quality of Service Management
  • Multitenant in RAC: CDBs, PDBs, PDB services and server pools, and automated PDB patching and relocation

The connections topic is the largest single topic on the page, with eight objective lines. That fits what happens on the job: users rarely notice a cluster until a node goes away and their session either survives or does not.

1Z0-078 Preparation Guide

The practitioner's advantage on this exam is that you can study it the way you would build it. A bottom-up plan means every new topic rests on one you have already worked through, and it keeps you from memorising RAC behaviour that you cannot explain.

Step 1: Build or borrow a lab you can break

Reading alone will not carry you through 77 questions on clustered systems. You need a two-node lab, or access to one, where you can stop Clusterware, pull a node, fill a disk group and watch what happens. Keep a log of each test. When a question later describes a symptom, you will have seen it.

Step 2: Start with Grid Infrastructure

Begin with the installation planning topics, because the exam asks about them directly and because they force you to understand the networks a cluster needs. Then install Grid Infrastructure and walk the startup sequence until you can explain what starts before what.

Spend real time on the OCR and voting files. Oracle's 19c documentation has a detail worth noticing here. The Clusterware guide says Clusterware files must be stored on ASM, yet the 19c changes page of the RAC Administration and Deployment Guide records that, starting with Grid Infrastructure 19c, the desupport of direct placement of OCR and voting files on shared file systems is rescinded for Oracle Standalone Clusters. Know both statements and which cluster type each applies to; that is exactly the kind of distinction a question can turn on.

Finish the layer with OCR backup and recovery, node addition and deletion, and policy-based management. Server pools come back later in the RAC topics, so understanding them here saves time.

Step 3: Move to ASM

Create disk groups at each redundancy level and look at the result. Oracle's ASM overview gives you rules you can test in a lab:

  • Normal redundancy disk groups require at least two failure groups, and high redundancy disk groups at least three.
  • If you omit the failure group specification, ASM places each disk in its own failure group (Exadata cells excepted).
  • You cannot alter the redundancy level of a disk group after it is created.
  • Allocation unit sizes can be 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 MB, depending on the disk group compatibility level.
  • ASM starts a rebalance automatically after you add, drop or resize disks, the power setting controls its speed, and databases can stay operational while it runs.

Then set up Flex ASM, change its cardinality, and work through ACFS: a volume, a file system on it, a snapshot, and at least one of the advanced features. The CloudFS topics hold nine objective lines between them, which is more than many candidates expect from the storage side.

Step 4: Finish with RAC

Now the RAC topics read as consequences of what sits underneath. Oracle's Introduction to Oracle RAC in the 19c RAC guide covers the ideas the exam builds on:

  • Cache Fusion uses the private interconnect for communication between instances, which is why the guide tells you not to use the interconnect for user traffic.
  • The Global Cache Service and the Global Enqueue Service coordinate buffer cache blocks and enqueues in the Global Resource Directory.
  • SCAN is a single network name, in DNS or Grid Naming Service, that round-robins to three IP addresses, and Oracle recommends that all client connections use it.
  • DBCA creates one default database service, which Oracle says should be reserved for maintenance; you create dynamic services for application connections.
  • RAC One Node runs a single instance of a RAC-enabled database on one node under normal operations, can relocate online with no downtime for users, and needs at least one dynamic database service.

Work the connection topics in the lab with a real client. Configure services, kill an instance, and watch what FAN, TAF and Application Continuity do. Then cover backup and recovery, tuning with AWR and ADDM, patching, and the multitenant topics.

Step 5: Read the objectives back as questions

In the last week, go through all 115 objective lines and turn each into a question you could answer out loud. "Explain the scope and capabilities of what-if command evaluation" becomes "what does SRVCTL evaluate mode report, and when would I run it?" Any line you cannot answer goes back to the lab.

Benefits and Career Scope of the 1Z0-078 Certification

The honest benefit of 1Z0-078 is that it names, in an employer's language, work that is otherwise hard to show on paper. A résumé line that says "supported RAC" can mean anything from running one SRVCTL command to rebuilding a cluster after a failed patch. An Oracle Certified Professional credential for RAC, ASM and Grid Infrastructure tells a reader that you were tested on the whole stack, including the storage and cluster layers that many database administrators never touch directly.

It also changes the work you get asked to do. Teams that run clustered Oracle databases need people who can plan an installation, patch Grid Infrastructure with minimal downtime, recover the OCR, and explain to an application team why their sessions dropped during a node failure. Those tasks map directly onto the exam topics, so preparing for the exam and becoming the person who handles those tickets are the same project.

There are limits worth stating. The credential is tied to Oracle Database 19c, and this article quotes no salary figures, because none comes from an official source. Oracle's exam page carried no retirement notice on 15 October 2026; check it again before you book, because Oracle updates its catalog.

The study itself has value even if you never sit the exam. Working through every objective line usually turns up at least one area, often ACFS, QoS Management or policy-based cluster management, that your current environment does not use and that you would otherwise meet for the first time during an incident.

Practice Test and Preparation Resources for 1Z0-078

Oracle's exam page links its recommended training. Three Oracle University courses on MyLearn line up with the three groupings of the syllabus, and their course pages show the module count and running time:

  • Oracle Database 19c: Clusterware Administration Workshop: 13 modules, 12 h 18 min, covering Clusterware architecture, cluster configuration options, preinstallation and installation, node management, policy-based management, patching, troubleshooting and application high availability.
  • Oracle Database 19c: ASM Administration Workshop: 13 modules, 8 h 7 min, covering ASM instances, Flex ASM, disk groups, files and templates, and ACFS with ADVM.
  • Oracle Database 19c: RAC Administration Workshop: 14 modules, 20 h 11 min, covering installation, administration, patching, backup and recovery, tuning, services, connection high availability, RAC One Node, multitenant and QoS in RAC.

Together that is about 40 hours of video before any lab time. Taken in the order listed, Clusterware first and RAC last, the courses follow the same bottom-up path as this article.

Oracle's documentation

The 19c guides are free and they are the source the exam objectives are written against. Keep three open while you study: the Clusterware Administration and Deployment Guide, the Automatic Storage Management Administrator's Guide, and the Real Application Clusters Administration and Deployment Guide. When a course and a guide seem to disagree, the guide for your exact release wins.

Practice questions

Once each layer is done, test it. The free 1Z0-078 sample questions on DBExam show the multiple-choice style and make a quick check after a study block. A full timed practice exam is the better rehearsal for the 93-second pace, and DBExam offers one for 1Z0-078 alongside the free set. Use the score report to send you back to specific topics rather than retaking until the number looks good.

A short video on working through answer options

The DBExam YouTube channel has no 1Z0-078 video yet. The walk-through below is about a different Oracle exam, 1Z0-149 on PL/SQL programming, but its method carries over: read every option, rule out the ones that contradict a documented fact, and only then choose.

Conclusion

1Z0-078 lists its 30 topics with RAC first, Grid Infrastructure second and ASM last. A working cluster is built the other way round, and the most reliable way to prepare is to follow the build: Clusterware and the OCR and voting files, then ASM disk groups, Flex ASM and ACFS, then the RAC database, its services and its clients.

The format is fixed and published: 77 multiple-choice questions, 120 minutes, a 65% passing score, delivered online with a proctor. The topic list is long but concrete, and almost every line can be practised in a two-node lab. If the work it describes is the work on your desk, the exam mostly asks you to prove you understand why that work is done the way it is.

FAQs

How many questions are on the 1Z0-078 exam, and how long do I get?

Oracle's exam page lists 77 multiple-choice questions, 120 minutes and a 65% passing score. That is about 93 seconds a question. The exam is delivered as Proctored Online.

Does Oracle publish topic weights for 1Z0-078?

No. The exam page lists 30 topics with 115 objective lines: 49 for RAC, 41 for Grid Infrastructure and 25 for ASM. Those are line counts, not percentages, so use them to judge coverage, not to predict how many questions each area will get.

Where can the OCR and voting files live in Grid Infrastructure 19c?

Oracle's Clusterware guide says both must sit on shared storage reachable by every node, and that Clusterware files must be stored on ASM. The 19c changes page of the RAC guide adds that, from Grid Infrastructure 19c, the desupport of placing OCR and voting files directly on shared file systems is rescinded for Oracle Standalone Clusters. Learn both statements and the cluster type each one covers.

What is the default number of ASM instances in Flex ASM?

Three. Oracle's Managing Oracle Flex ASM chapter says the number of ASM instances is set with a cardinality setting and that the default is three instances. You can change it with SRVCTL.

event_model_payload.summary:
If you run Oracle databases on more than one server, you already know the order things happen in on a real cluster. Someone prepares the operating system, the shared disks and the networks. Then Grid Infrastructure goes on, which brings Oracle Clusterware and Oracle Automatic Storage Management with it. Only after that does anyone install the database software, and only after that does a RAC database exist to tune, patch and connect to.

Oracle's exam page for 1Z0-078 lists the same material in the opposite order. It starts with RAC databases and architecture, moves on to Grid Infrastructure in the middle, and ends with ASM disk groups, files and the ASM Cluster File System. That is a fine way to describe a job. It is a poor way to learn one, because almost every RAC objective assumes you understand the layers underneath it.

This article follows the build order instead. It is written for the DBA or systems administrator who already looks after clustered databases and wants to know whether 1Z0-078 matches the work on their desk. Every number in it comes from Oracle's own exam page and Oracle's 19c documentation, both checked on 15 October 2026.

What Is the Oracle 1Z0-078 RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Exam?

1Z0-078 is the exam behind the Oracle Certified Professional, Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administrator credential. Its full title on Oracle MyLearn is "Exam 1Z0-078: Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administration", and the official 1Z0-078 exam page on Oracle MyLearn is where the topic list, the format and the session rules live.

Oracle describes the audience plainly. The certification is for database production systems administrators and database administrators with 12 to 18 months of experience using RAC, ASM and Grid Infrastructure. The exam measures installation, configuration, backup and recovery, monitoring and tuning of those components. Read that as a description of who does well, not as an entry rule: the page states an experience profile, and it is worth being honest with yourself about whether you match it.

The three names in the title are three layers of one stack, and it helps to be precise about how they relate, because the exam is.

Grid Infrastructure: the base layer

Oracle's Introduction to Oracle Clusterware in the 19c Clusterware Administration and Deployment Guide explains that Clusterware lets separate servers communicate so they appear to applications and users as one system. Since Oracle Clusterware 12c, the Clusterware and ASM binaries are installed as a single binary called Oracle Grid Infrastructure. The same guide notes that Clusterware 19c supports only ASM 19c, because ASM sits in the Grid Infrastructure home that also holds Clusterware.

Clusterware keeps two stored components besides its binaries. Voting files record node membership. The Oracle Cluster Registry, or OCR, records cluster configuration: databases, listeners, virtual IP addresses, services and any applications Clusterware manages. Both must sit on shared storage that every cluster node can reach.

ASM: the storage layer

ASM is Oracle's volume manager and file system for database files. Oracle's overview chapter of the 19c ASM Administrator's Guide describes disk groups made of disks, files and allocation units, with normal redundancy giving two-way mirroring, high redundancy three-way mirroring, and external redundancy leaving the mirroring to a RAID subsystem.

RAC: the database layer

Oracle RAC lets several instances open one database. The RAC guide says that having multiple instances access a single database prevents the server from being a single point of failure, and that applications deployed on RAC databases can operate without code changes. RAC depends on Clusterware; the guide calls Clusterware a required component that provides the infrastructure RAC runs on.

So the order on the exam page is top-down, while the order on a real system is bottom-up. Hold on to that idea. It shapes the study plan later in this article.

1Z0-078 Exam Overview and Details

The format is short to state. Everything below is from Oracle's exam page unless marked otherwise.

  • Exam code: 1Z0-078
  • Exam name: Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administration
  • Credential: Oracle Certified Professional, Oracle Database 19c: RAC, ASM, and Grid Infrastructure Administrator
  • Delivery: Proctored Online
  • Format: Multiple Choice
  • Duration: 120 minutes
  • Number of questions: 77
  • Passing score: 65%
  • Price: Oracle's page shows no price to a signed-out visitor. The DBExam syllabus page lists USD $245 and notes that pricing may vary by country or local currency; confirm the figure in your Oracle account at checkout.

What 77 questions in 120 minutes means at the desk

120 minutes across 77 questions is about 93 seconds a question. That is generous for a question that asks you to recognise a view name and tight for one that describes a failed node, a set of services and a client configuration, then asks what the client sees. Plan to move quickly through recall questions so the scenario questions get the time they need.

A 65% passing score on 77 questions works out to just over 50 correct answers, if every question counts the same. Oracle does not publish how it weights individual questions, so treat 51 as a planning number rather than a rule, and aim well above it.

Session rules worth knowing in advance

  • A government-issued identification is required to take the exam.
  • Check-in time is 30 minutes before the exam time.
  • Your computer must meet Oracle's minimum system requirements for online proctoring.
  • Results are shown on screen at the close of the exam, and the detailed score report is in Oracle CertView.
  • To reschedule, you must do it at least 24 hours before your appointment time.

None of these is unusual, but the 30-minute check-in catches people who block exactly two hours in their calendar. Block three.

Key Topics and Syllabus for 1Z0-078

Oracle's exam page lists 30 topics and 115 objective lines under three groupings. The first grouping has no heading of its own on the page; it is the RAC material. Then come the headings "Grid Infrastructure Administration" and "Automatic Storage Management (ASM) Administration". Counted line by line:

  • RAC administration: 12 topics, 49 objective lines
  • Grid Infrastructure administration: 11 topics, 41 objective lines
  • ASM administration: 7 topics, 25 objective lines

One caution before you use those counts: Oracle publishes no percentage weights for 1Z0-078. A line count shows where the page spends its words, not how many questions each area gets. The 1Z0-078 syllabus on DBExam sets the same topics out on one page with the exam facts beside them, which is handy as a checklist.

Here is the syllabus in the order you would build the system, bottom layer first.

Layer 1: Grid Infrastructure and Clusterware (11 topics)

The Grid Infrastructure grouping covers the life of the cluster itself:

  • Introduction to Clusterware and Oracle Clusterware architecture, including startup details and how Grid Plug and Play affects Clusterware
  • Flex Clusters and the effect of node failure in one
  • Installation planning and pre-tasks: system and network requirements, groups, users and directories
  • Grid Infrastructure installation, verifying it, configuring ASM disk groups, and the optional Grid Infrastructure Management Repository
  • Managing cluster nodes: extending a cluster, deleting a node, and adding nodes with DBCA
  • Traditional Clusterware management: day-to-day tasks, OCR backup and recovery, network settings, what-if command evaluation and secure cluster communication
  • Policy-based cluster management: server categorization, policy sets and activating a policy
  • Upgrading and patching Grid Infrastructure, including rolling patches and zero-downtime Grid Infrastructure patching
  • Troubleshooting Clusterware: log files, diagcollection.pl, resource and component debugging, and OCR problems
  • Making applications highly available with Clusterware: policy-managed and administrator-managed databases, application VIPs and application resources

Two documented facts from this layer tend to matter. First, Oracle recommends no more than five voting files, although Clusterware supports up to 15. Second, you can have up to five OCR locations, and you can replace a failed OCR location online as long as it is not the only one. Small numbers like these make good exam distractors, so learn them exactly.

Flex Clusters have their own rules in the Clusterware Administration and Deployment Guide: a Flex Cluster can have as many as 64 Hub Nodes, Hub Nodes have direct access to shared storage and host read-write instances, other nodes request data through Hub Nodes and host read-only instances, Flex Clusters require Grid Naming Service, and you can convert a standard cluster to a Flex Cluster but not the reverse.

Layer 2: ASM, ACFS and ADVM (7 topics)

The ASM grouping is the shortest, but it sits under everything else:

  • ASM architecture and components
  • ASM instances: initialization parameters, processes, and monitoring with the V$ASM dynamic performance views
  • Flex ASM: architecture, installation, configuration and management
  • Disk groups: creating, dropping, setting attributes, maintenance, and performance and scalability considerations
  • Files, directories and templates, including the format of a fully qualified ASM file name
  • Oracle CloudFS: the ASM Dynamic Volume Manager, ASM volumes, ACFS and ACFS snapshots
  • CloudFS advanced topics: ACFS auditing, encryption, replication and tagging, and High Availability NFS

The file name objective is a good example of how literal the exam can be. Oracle's chapter on ASM files, directories and templates gives the form as +diskgroup/dbname/filetype/filetypetag.file.incarnation in a non-multitenant database, and +diskgroup/cdb/pdb_guid/filetype/filetypetag.file.incarnation with multitenant. Alias names are told apart because they do not end in a dotted pair of numbers. If you can read +DATA/ORCL/DATAFILE/system.257.967544915 and name every field, that objective is done.

Flex ASM gets three objective lines. The key documented behaviour is in Oracle's Managing Oracle Flex ASM chapter: a small set of ASM instances serves the whole cluster, the number is set with a cardinality setting, and the default is three instances. The ASM overview adds why it matters: in a standard ASM cluster, if the ASM instance on a node fails, the database instances on that node fail too, while with Flex ASM a database instance can reach another ASM instance on another node.

Layer 3: The RAC database (12 topics)

RAC gets the most objective lines, and it is where most candidates already feel at home:

  • RAC architecture: the benefits of RAC, why global resources are needed, and global cache coordination
  • Installing and configuring RAC, creating a cluster database, and converting a single-instance database to RAC
  • Administering RAC: redo log files, undo tablespaces, starting and stopping, and initialization parameters
  • Backup and recovery: ARCHIVELOG mode, the fast recovery area, and RMAN in a RAC environment
  • Global resources: the Global Resource Directory, global enqueue and instance locks, global buffer cache management, and affinity
  • Monitoring and tuning: RAC wait events, AWR and ADDM in RAC, the Cluster Database Performance pages, and SGA runtime management
  • High availability of services, and high availability for connections and applications: load balancing, the Load Balancing Advisory, FAN, TAF, Transparent Application Continuity and Dynamic Services Fallback
  • Upgrading and patching RAC with OUI and opatch
  • RAC One Node conversions in both directions
  • Quality of Service Management
  • Multitenant in RAC: CDBs, PDBs, PDB services and server pools, and automated PDB patching and relocation

The connections topic is the largest single topic on the page, with eight objective lines. That fits what happens on the job: users rarely notice a cluster until a node goes away and their session either survives or does not.

1Z0-078 Preparation Guide

The practitioner's advantage on this exam is that you can study it the way you would build it. A bottom-up plan means every new topic rests on one you have already worked through, and it keeps you from memorising RAC behaviour that you cannot explain.

Step 1: Build or borrow a lab you can break

Reading alone will not carry you through 77 questions on clustered systems. You need a two-node lab, or access to one, where you can stop Clusterware, pull a node, fill a disk group and watch what happens. Keep a log of each test. When a question later describes a symptom, you will have seen it.

Step 2: Start with Grid Infrastructure

Begin with the installation planning topics, because the exam asks about them directly and because they force you to understand the networks a cluster needs. Then install Grid Infrastructure and walk the startup sequence until you can explain what starts before what.

Spend real time on the OCR and voting files. Oracle's 19c documentation has a detail worth noticing here. The Clusterware guide says Clusterware files must be stored on ASM, yet the 19c changes page of the RAC Administration and Deployment Guide records that, starting with Grid Infrastructure 19c, the desupport of direct placement of OCR and voting files on shared file systems is rescinded for Oracle Standalone Clusters. Know both statements and which cluster type each applies to; that is exactly the kind of distinction a question can turn on.

Finish the layer with OCR backup and recovery, node addition and deletion, and policy-based management. Server pools come back later in the RAC topics, so understanding them here saves time.

Step 3: Move to ASM

Create disk groups at each redundancy level and look at the result. Oracle's ASM overview gives you rules you can test in a lab:

  • Normal redundancy disk groups require at least two failure groups, and high redundancy disk groups at least three.
  • If you omit the failure group specification, ASM places each disk in its own failure group (Exadata cells excepted).
  • You cannot alter the redundancy level of a disk group after it is created.
  • Allocation unit sizes can be 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 or 64 MB, depending on the disk group compatibility level.
  • ASM starts a rebalance automatically after you add, drop or resize disks, the power setting controls its speed, and databases can stay operational while it runs.

Then set up Flex ASM, change its cardinality, and work through ACFS: a volume, a file system on it, a snapshot, and at least one of the advanced features. The CloudFS topics hold nine objective lines between them, which is more than many candidates expect from the storage side.

Step 4: Finish with RAC

Now the RAC topics read as consequences of what sits underneath. Oracle's Introduction to Oracle RAC in the 19c RAC guide covers the ideas the exam builds on:

  • Cache Fusion uses the private interconnect for communication between instances, which is why the guide tells you not to use the interconnect for user traffic.
  • The Global Cache Service and the Global Enqueue Service coordinate buffer cache blocks and enqueues in the Global Resource Directory.
  • SCAN is a single network name, in DNS or Grid Naming Service, that round-robins to three IP addresses, and Oracle recommends that all client connections use it.
  • DBCA creates one default database service, which Oracle says should be reserved for maintenance; you create dynamic services for application connections.
  • RAC One Node runs a single instance of a RAC-enabled database on one node under normal operations, can relocate online with no downtime for users, and needs at least one dynamic database service.

Work the connection topics in the lab with a real client. Configure services, kill an instance, and watch what FAN, TAF and Application Continuity do. Then cover backup and recovery, tuning with AWR and ADDM, patching, and the multitenant topics.

Step 5: Read the objectives back as questions

In the last week, go through all 115 objective lines and turn each into a question you could answer out loud. "Explain the scope and capabilities of what-if command evaluation" becomes "what does SRVCTL evaluate mode report, and when would I run it?" Any line you cannot answer goes back to the lab.

Benefits and Career Scope of the 1Z0-078 Certification

The honest benefit of 1Z0-078 is that it names, in an employer's language, work that is otherwise hard to show on paper. A résumé line that says "supported RAC" can mean anything from running one SRVCTL command to rebuilding a cluster after a failed patch. An Oracle Certified Professional credential for RAC, ASM and Grid Infrastructure tells a reader that you were tested on the whole stack, including the storage and cluster layers that many database administrators never touch directly.

It also changes the work you get asked to do. Teams that run clustered Oracle databases need people who can plan an installation, patch Grid Infrastructure with minimal downtime, recover the OCR, and explain to an application team why their sessions dropped during a node failure. Those tasks map directly onto the exam topics, so preparing for the exam and becoming the person who handles those tickets are the same project.

There are limits worth stating. The credential is tied to Oracle Database 19c, and this article quotes no salary figures, because none comes from an official source. Oracle's exam page carried no retirement notice on 15 October 2026; check it again before you book, because Oracle updates its catalog.

The study itself has value even if you never sit the exam. Working through every objective line usually turns up at least one area, often ACFS, QoS Management or policy-based cluster management, that your current environment does not use and that you would otherwise meet for the first time during an incident.

Practice Test and Preparation Resources for 1Z0-078

Oracle's exam page links its recommended training. Three Oracle University courses on MyLearn line up with the three groupings of the syllabus, and their course pages show the module count and running time:

  • Oracle Database 19c: Clusterware Administration Workshop: 13 modules, 12 h 18 min, covering Clusterware architecture, cluster configuration options, preinstallation and installation, node management, policy-based management, patching, troubleshooting and application high availability.
  • Oracle Database 19c: ASM Administration Workshop: 13 modules, 8 h 7 min, covering ASM instances, Flex ASM, disk groups, files and templates, and ACFS with ADVM.
  • Oracle Database 19c: RAC Administration Workshop: 14 modules, 20 h 11 min, covering installation, administration, patching, backup and recovery, tuning, services, connection high availability, RAC One Node, multitenant and QoS in RAC.

Together that is about 40 hours of video before any lab time. Taken in the order listed, Clusterware first and RAC last, the courses follow the same bottom-up path as this article.

Oracle's documentation

The 19c guides are free and they are the source the exam objectives are written against. Keep three open while you study: the Clusterware Administration and Deployment Guide, the Automatic Storage Management Administrator's Guide, and the Real Application Clusters Administration and Deployment Guide. When a course and a guide seem to disagree, the guide for your exact release wins.

Practice questions

Once each layer is done, test it. The free 1Z0-078 sample questions on DBExam show the multiple-choice style and make a quick check after a study block. A full timed practice exam is the better rehearsal for the 93-second pace, and DBExam offers one for 1Z0-078 alongside the free set. Use the score report to send you back to specific topics rather than retaking until the number looks good.

A short video on working through answer options

The DBExam YouTube channel has no 1Z0-078 video yet. The walk-through below is about a different Oracle exam, 1Z0-149 on PL/SQL programming, but its method carries over: read every option, rule out the ones that contradict a documented fact, and only then choose.

Conclusion

1Z0-078 lists its 30 topics with RAC first, Grid Infrastructure second and ASM last. A working cluster is built the other way round, and the most reliable way to prepare is to follow the build: Clusterware and the OCR and voting files, then ASM disk groups, Flex ASM and ACFS, then the RAC database, its services and its clients.

The format is fixed and published: 77 multiple-choice questions, 120 minutes, a 65% passing score, delivered online with a proctor. The topic list is long but concrete, and almost every line can be practised in a two-node lab. If the work it describes is the work on your desk, the exam mostly asks you to prove you understand why that work is done the way it is.

FAQs

Oracle's exam page lists 77 multiple-choice questions, 120 minutes and a 65% passing score. That is about 93 seconds a question. The exam is delivered as Proctored Online.

No. The exam page lists 30 topics with 115 objective lines: 49 for RAC, 41 for Grid Infrastructure and 25 for ASM. Those are line counts, not percentages, so use them to judge coverage, not to predict how many questions each area will get.

Where can the OCR and voting files live in Grid Infrastructure 19c?

Oracle's Clusterware guide says both must sit on shared storage reachable by every node, and that Clusterware files must be stored on ASM. The 19c changes page of the RAC guide adds that, from Grid Infrastructure 19c, the desupport of placing OCR and voting files directly on shared file systems is rescinded for Oracle Standalone Clusters. Three. Oracle's Managing Oracle Flex ASM chapter says the number of ASM instances is set with a cardinality setting and that the default is three instances. You can change it with SRVCTL.

The exam page offers recommended training: the Clusterware, ASM and RAC administration workshops on MyLearn, about 40 hours combined. The page does not state a course requirement. Check Oracle's Certification Program Guidelines for the credential before you book.

What should I bring to the online 1Z0-078 session?

A government-issued identification, a computer that meets Oracle's minimum system requirements, and a testing space that meets Oracle's rules. Check in 30 minutes before the exam time. Your result appears on screen at the end, and the detailed score report is in Oracle CertView. If you need to reschedule, do it at least 24 hours before your appointment.

title: Your Cloud App Is Live. Can You Tell When Something Goes Wrong?
summary:
Your application is deployed. The page loads, the API responds, and your latest release looks successful.

But what happens an hour later?

An endpoint starts slowing down. Requests fail intermittently. Storage usage keeps growing.

The next cloud skill worth learning is monitoring: understanding what your application is doing after deployment.

Start with three questions

Before creating a dashboard, decide what you need to know:

  1. Is the application available?
  2. Is it responding quickly enough?
  3. Are users experiencing errors?

These questions give your monitoring a purpose.

For a small API, start by tracking request volume, response time, and error rate. Add infrastructure metrics, such as CPU usage, where they help explain application behavior.

Understand metrics, logs, and traces

These tools answer different questions:

  • Metrics show patterns over time, such as rising response times or a sudden increase in failed requests.
  • Logs record events that can help explain what happened during a failure.
  • Traces follow requests across components, helping you identify where time was spent or an error occurred.

Imagine your API becomes slow.

A response-time metric shows when the slowdown started. Application logs reveal repeated database timeouts. A trace helps identify the database call responsible for the delay.

You can introduce these tools gradually as your project grows.

Make alerts useful

An alert should point to something you can investigate or act on.

For a learning project, consider alerts for:

  • Repeated failed health checks.
  • A sustained increase in server errors.
  • Response times exceeding your chosen threshold.
  • Spending approaching your budget.

Choose thresholds based on your application’s normal behavior. Too many noisy alerts make it harder to notice the ones that matter.

For each alert, write a short note: what it means, where to investigate, and what recovery steps to try.

Practise a controlled failure

Use a test environment to stop your application deliberately.

Check whether your monitoring detects the failure. Inspect the logs, restore the service, and verify that it becomes healthy again.

Record what you learned in your project README.

Deploying an application is a milestone. Knowing how to detect and recover from a failure builds confidence in running it.

title: Your App Runs in Docker. Now Automate the Next Step with CI/CD.
summary:
You’ve deployed an application on AWS and learned how Docker packages it into a repeatable environment.

Then you change a few lines of code.

Now you need to run the tests, rebuild the image, and deploy the updated version. Doing that manually for every change can become repetitive—and makes it easy to miss a step.

This is a good time to learn CI/CD.

What does CI/CD mean?

Continuous Integration (CI) means integrating code changes frequently, with automated builds and tests to catch problems early.

For example, when you open a pull request, a workflow can:

  • Install the project’s dependencies.
  • Check formatting and code quality.
  • Run automated tests.
  • Verify that the application builds successfully.

Continuous Delivery keeps validated changes ready for release, with a possible manual approval before production.

Continuous Deployment goes further: changes that pass the required checks are automatically released to production.

Start with one useful workflow

For your first pipeline, choose an application you already understand.

A practical starting point is:

Open a pull request → run tests → check the result → review and merge.

Before automating anything, make sure your tests run successfully on your own machine. Then configure your CI platform to run the same test command.

Try making a change that deliberately breaks a test. Open a pull request and inspect the failure.

Fix the problem and watch the checks pass.

That exercise gives you a clear understanding of what your pipeline protects—and what it doesn’t.

Add Docker after your checks work

Once the test workflow is reliable, add a step that builds your Docker image.

Later, extend the process to publish the image to a registry and deploy it to a test environment.

Use a unique version tag, such as the commit identifier, so you can connect a deployed image to its source code.

Before automating production releases, decide:

  • How will you verify that the updated application is healthy?
  • Where will deployment credentials be stored securely?
  • How will you restore the previous version if something fails?

A useful pipeline makes failures visible and successful releases repeatable.

In May 2026, Anthropic merged about 2,500 code changes per day into its monorepo. By September, that number was 30,000. A 12x surge in four months — driven almost entirely by Claude agents writing, testing, and shipping code. The developer infrastructure that had served human engineers for years buckled under the weight. Git, the version control system that underpins nearly every software team on the planet, could not keep up.

📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on ComputeLeap →

So Anthropic did something radical: it replaced Git entirely. A seven-person team spent five months building Scion, a custom version control system designed from scratch for agent-scale development, plus Antique, a companion code review tool. They migrated their entire monorepo — nearly 100 GB of main-branch history — off Git and onto the new system.

View original post on X →

This is not a theoretical exercise or a conference talk about what might happen. This is a production migration at one of the most important AI companies in the world, and it carries a clear signal for every engineering team running coding agents: your infrastructure was built for humans. When agents arrive at scale, something will break. The question is what, and whether you have planned for it.

What Actually Broke

Git's core design dates to 2005, when Linus Torvalds built it for Linux kernel development. Its fundamental assumption is that every clone is a complete, offline-capable copy of the repository. That is elegant for distributed human teams. It is catastrophic for thousands of always-online agents.

Here is what Anthropic hit as merge volume climbed:

The mirror problem. To serve thousands of concurrent agents, CI jobs, and research workloads, Anthropic ran several hundred internal Git mirrors. Each mirror holds a full copy of the repo. As merge rates climbed, keeping mirrors in sync became untenable — seeds drifted from main between refreshes, diff and blame on partial clones produced incorrect results, and mirrors started exceeding their disk and memory limits.

The checkout explosion. At peak, Anthropic's CI infrastructure ran roughly 25 million checkouts per day — excluding developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. A naive fetch model implied over 600 petabytes of Git traffic daily. Standard workarounds (shallow clones, sparse checkouts, promisor remotes, blob-stored seeds) helped temporarily but became increasingly fragile.

The merge queue bottleneck. A traditional merge queue uses a global lock: changes enter a serialized queue, CI validates each one, and they merge to main in order. At human scale (tens of merges per hour), this works. At agent scale (30,000+ per day), a global lock becomes a throughput ceiling. As Amplify Partners noted, Git's reconciliation algorithms max out at roughly 2-3 merges to main per second in baseline configurations.

Read the full engineering post on Anthropic →

Scion: What Anthropic Built

Scion inverts Git's core assumptions. Where Git assumes clients work offline and keep full copies, Scion assumes clients are always online — because nearly all of them are agents and CI jobs.

Server-side operations. The Scion server handles history queries, blame, commits, merges, and rebases. Clients keep a bounded local cache, track filesystem changes, and provide the user interface — but the heavy computation stays server-side. Creating a commit scales with the size of the change, not the size of the repository.

API-first design. Every source control query goes through an API. This means many CI jobs and automated pipelines never need a local checkout at all. Automated bisect and revert pipelines depend entirely on API calls, not local clones.

Three-tier caching. Scion uses a layered cache architecture:

  1. scion-daemon — one per compute node, shared by all jobs on that node, bootstrapped from periodic snapshots
  2. scion-cache — regional caches that stream objects from memory
  3. scion-server — authoritative, backed by Google Spanner and cloud storage

All three tiers share the same RPCs, so clients do not need to know the topology. Each tier maintains over 99% cache hit rates. Failure domains are strictly isolated — a regional cache failure cannot overwhelm upstream servers.

Changesets, not commits. Scion's unit of work is a changeset — an entry in a write-ahead log that records files changed relative to the first parent, with content-addressed pointers to compressed blobs. In trunk-based development, mainline history is what matters most, and Scion's data model reflects that.

Refs are discouraged. Unlike Git, where branches and tags are cheap and abundant, Scion actively discourages refs beyond main and release branches. The reason: globally shared state creates scaling problems when thousands of agents are operating concurrently.

The Results

Anthropic's performance claims are striking, though they come from Anthropic itself and have not been independently verified:

💡 Scion uses approximately 200x less CPU and memory than Anthropic's previous fleet of several hundred Git mirrors. CI checkouts dropped from minutes to seconds — roughly two orders of magnitude faster. CI alone gained a 25% CPU capacity win. Every cache tier maintains over 99% hit rates with no long-lived state.

Perhaps the most telling detail: Claude itself rewrote the Git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline. Anthropic reports the Claude-written version used 20x less memory and ran 4x faster than the handwritten prototype, while preserving ingestion-ordering invariants. Claude also found an algorithmic optimization to ancestry queries that had eluded the human engineers — it noticed an existing index that was not being used.

The Self-Referential Loop Nobody Is Talking About

Here is what most coverage of Scion misses: this is a story about AI building its own infrastructure.

Claude agents generated the code volume that broke Git. Claude agents then helped build the replacement. Claude agents now monitor Scion's health through "superfan" bots that watch individual components' telemetry and logs, supplementing traditional alerts. And Claude agents are the primary users of the new system.

The Register framed it bluntly: the bottleneck was self-inflicted. Claude generated the code volume, and Claude was then used to fix the tooling. That is not criticism — it is a preview of what agent-driven engineering looks like. The toolchain becomes part of the product's own feedback loop.

This matters because it changes the economics of developer infrastructure. When your agents generate enough load to justify custom infrastructure, and your agents can help build that infrastructure, the ROI calculation shifts dramatically. The seven-person team that built Scion was leveraging Claude throughout — engineers focused on system design and trade-offs while Claude handled implementation.

Read the full analysis on DevOps.com →

GitHub's Response: Rebuilding in Place

Anthropic had the luxury of a clean-sheet design. GitHub does not. With over 200 million developers (and an exponentially growing population of agents) on its platform, GitHub is rebuilding its Git backend in place — while keeping the service running.

The numbers tell the same story from a different angle. Brian Celenza, a principal engineer on GitHub's storage team, published the scale of what they are facing:

  • Pushes grew 4.9x year over year, from 0.69 billion to 3.35 billion per month
  • 7.38 billion commits in September 2026 alone, over 5x the prior year
  • GitHub Actions ran 3.26 billion times in September, also 4x year-over-year
  • Total Git activity more than doubled, from 218.2 billion to 473.3 billion events per month

GitHub's COO Kyle Daigle told Latent Space he expects 14 billion commits for 2026, up from about 1 billion in all of 2025.

GitHub's architecture fix mirrors some of Scion's principles. The current Spokes system stores full replicas on local disks, with every replica participating in every write. The new architecture decouples storage (Azure Blob Storage) from compute (stateless cache workers), with internal benchmarks showing up to 35x higher write throughput. Losing a compute worker becomes a cache miss, not a data loss event.

The key difference: GitHub must preserve backward compatibility with Git's protocol, ecosystem, and user expectations. Anthropic threw all of that away.

The Broader Version Control War

Anthropic and GitHub are not alone in rethinking version control for agents. A small but serious cohort of startups is attacking the problem from different angles.

GitButler, founded by GitHub co-founder Scott Chacon, raised $17M from a16z to build agent-optimized version control. Their bet: Git's porcelain (the user-facing commands) is the bottleneck, not the plumbing. GitButler supports parallel branches, agent-specific CLI commands, and rich metadata tracking. Their experimental project Grit — a from-scratch rewrite of Git in Rust, largely built by AI agents — demonstrates the approach.

East River Source Control (backed by Amplify Partners, led by Steve Klabnik) is building a new backend that swaps Git's storage engine for a horizontally scalable alternative while keeping the Git protocol and Jujutsu as the interface. Their argument: Git's distributed model is right, but its storage ceiling is the constraint.

Entire is building a distributed repository network with synchronized mirrors closer to agents, arguing that centralized hosting platforms are themselves the bottleneck. Their Field CTO Karthik Rameshkumar's WeAreDevelopers talk titled "Fixing Git for Agents" summarized the position: traditional version control is fundamentally broken for AI coding agents.

What the Community Is Saying

The developer community's reaction has been split between admiration and skepticism.

The Hacker News thread — 873 points and nearly 1,000 comments — became one of the most active engineering discussions of the week, with practitioners debating whether Scion validates or undermines the case for Git at scale.

View the full discussion on Hacker News →

On Bluesky, developer Nick Gerakines wrote: "Git had been and continues to be bad for mono repo development at large scale." Tim Kellogg noted that Anthropic's decision to abandon the single global merge queue was the most significant architectural choice.

Read the full coverage on AI Weekly →

On X, the announcement drew wide commentary. AGTP Insights summarized the split: some see Scion as the end of Git for large-scale agent operations, while skeptics question whether anyone can meaningfully track 30,000 changes per day.

View original post on X →

On the skeptical side, developer Austin Parker observed: "You can sure do neat stuff when you buy tokens by the truckload." And that is a fair point — Anthropic's internal token spend far exceeds typical business usage, which is part of why a clean-sheet VCS redesign is practical for them and not for most teams.

View original post on X →

Mitch Ashley of The Futurum Group put it in strategic terms: "Source control has joined the fight over agent-driven software delivery." He drew a parallel to NVIDIA's Hugging Face deal, arguing that AI leaders are racing to own infrastructure — not just models.

⚠️ The "git is dead" narrative is premature. Anthropic built Scion for a monorepo approaching 100 GB with 30,000+ daily merges — a problem roughly seven companies on Earth actually have. For 99.9% of teams, the real bottleneck is not Git itself but the human review workflows wrapped around it. GitHub is already rebuilding its backend with 35x higher write throughput while preserving full backward compatibility. Bet on Git adapting before betting on Git dying.

Prior Art: This Is Not New Territory

Anthropic is not the first company to outgrow Git. Google built Piper, a centralized VCS holding over two billion lines of code, described publicly in 2016. Meta built Sapling, later open-sourced, which keeps Git's conceptual model but redesigns the storage and user interface. Both were responses to the same fundamental tension: Git's distributed model assumes each user maintains a full copy, which becomes untenable at extreme scale.

What is new is the speed. Google and Meta evolved their systems over years as human engineering teams grew. Anthropic hit the wall in four months because agents do not ramp up gradually — they scale with compute.

What This Means for You

Most teams will not build their own VCS. But if you are running coding agents today — Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Codex — Anthropic's experience is an early warning. Here is the infrastructure audit:

💡 Three questions every team running coding agents should answer:

  1. Merge queue serialization: Can your merge process handle 100+ concurrent merges? If you are using a single-threaded merge queue, it will become your bottleneck before anything else does.

  2. CI fan-out ratio: Each agent push triggers CI, which triggers clones, which triggers read amplification. What is your read fan-out per write? At agent scale, this can be 1,000:1 or higher.

  3. Repository growth rate: Agents checkpoint constantly, inflating commit history. Track your repo size growth weekly. If it is accelerating, you need a strategy — shallow clones, sparse checkouts, or periodic history rewriting.

Anthropic's post suggests that Git platforms could adopt some of Scion's ideas — server-side RPCs, novel negotiation protocols, and sparse/shallow features that compose better. GitHub is already moving in this direction. The gap between "what Git was designed for" and "what agents demand" will only widen.

Read the detailed analysis on CellCog →

The era of developer infrastructure designed for human-speed collaboration is ending. What replaces it is still being built — by seven-person teams at Anthropic, by GitHub's storage engineers, and by a growing cohort of startups who see version control as the next battleground. For practitioners, the takeaway is simpler: audit your infrastructure now, while you still have time to adapt.

title: Choosing a Termius Alternative: Match the Client to Your SSH Workflow
summary:
Replacing an SSH client is easy to regret if you compare only terminal screenshots. The real question is which parts of your workflow you need to keep: mobile access, saved hosts, graphical file transfers, port forwarding, or tools for working on the server after you connect.

Termius already has a free Starter plan with SSH, SFTP, and port forwarding. Its paid plans add features such as a personal cloud vault and device synchronization. If those free features are all you use, switching may not solve a problem. If you rely on synced hosts or mobile access, a desktop-only alternative may be a downgrade even if it costs less.

Start with the job you need the client to do

Write down what you actually do in a typical session. For example:

  • Connect to a few servers from one Windows machine.
  • Open several terminal sessions and keep them organized.
  • Upload files through a graphical SFTP browser.
  • Forward a port to reach a service on a remote server.
  • Connect from a phone when away from your computer.
  • Share hosts or credentials with a team.

These needs point to different tools. “Supports SSH” is only a starting point: it does not tell you whether an app has graphical SFTP, a mobile app, team controls, or a convenient way to manage tunnels.

A useful distinction: SFTP support is not the same as a graphical SFTP file manager. OpenSSH provides command-line tools such as sftp; a client with a visual file browser is a better fit if you want to drag and drop files. Similarly, SSH port forwarding carries traffic through an SSH connection; it is not the same thing as an embedded remote-desktop client.

Match the alternative to your setup

You want a free desktop terminal

Tabby is a free, open-source terminal for Windows, macOS, and Linux. It offers SSH sessions, tabs, split panes, and customization through plugins. It is a reasonable choice if you want a configurable desktop workflow and do not need Termius-style synced hosts across desktop and mobile devices.

Tabby is based on Electron, and its maintainers do not describe it as lightweight. Choose it for its features and customization rather than assuming it will use fewer resources than another client.

You need SSH, graphical SFTP, and tunnels on Windows

Bitvise SSH Client is a free Windows option with SSH, a graphical SFTP interface, and port-forwarding features. The client is free for use in business environments too; its optional paid license concerns support and upgrade commitments. Bitvise SSH Server is separate software, so do not confuse the client’s terms with the server’s.

MobaXterm may fit if your Windows toolbox also needs RDP, VNC, or an X server for displaying remote Linux GUI applications. Its free Home edition has limits, so check the current edition terms before adopting it for a team or a larger set of sessions.

You mostly transfer files

WinSCP is designed around file transfers rather than being a full SSH terminal manager. It supports graphical transfers, scripting, and directory synchronization. If you mainly connect to upload releases or manage remote files, that focus may be an advantage. If you also need interactive terminal sessions, pair it with an SSH client or choose a tool that combines both workflows.

You want a minimal, command-line setup

Windows includes OpenSSH as an optional feature, and it is commonly available on Linux and macOS. You can connect directly from a terminal:

ssh user@server.example.com

For repeated connections, a host entry in your SSH config can save the hostname, user, port, and identity file. The SSH config file examples show how to organize those settings and connect with a short alias. OpenSSH is a good fit if you prefer ordinary text configuration over a graphical host manager; it does not provide a graphical SFTP browser by itself.

Treat migration as a security task

A saved host entry, a private key, an agent-loaded identity, and a team vault are different things. Do not assume one client can import all of them automatically. Record the host, username, port, key choice, jump-host settings, and any tunnels you depend on. Then test a few important connections in the new client before changing your existing setup.

Keep private keys private. Do not paste them into chat, tickets, or repositories to make migration easier. If you are moving or replacing keys, plan access and revocation deliberately; this overview of SSH key management covers the key lifecycle and the risks of leaving stale credentials in place.

Also verify server identity when connecting through a new client. If it warns that a host key has changed unexpectedly, investigate the change rather than accepting it just to finish setup. A successful password or key login does not, on its own, establish that you reached the intended server.

A practical decision checklist

Before settling on an alternative, test it with a non-critical host and answer these questions:

  1. Can it use the authentication method and key you need?
  2. Does it provide a graphical SFTP interface if you want one?
  3. Can it reproduce your jump-host and port-forwarding workflow?
  4. Does it run on every device you use, including your phone if necessary?
  5. Are host sync and team sharing included, and do they meet your security requirements?
  6. Can you get your configuration and credentials back if you lose access to the app or device?

If you only need occasional terminal access, OpenSSH or PuTTY may be enough. For free Windows SSH with graphical file transfer and tunneling, consider Bitvise. For a customizable cross-platform terminal, try Tabby. For mobile access and synchronized hosts, check that the replacement actually offers those capabilities before leaving Termius.

The best alternative is not the one with the longest feature list. It is the one that preserves the parts of your SSH workflow you rely on—and does not make you pay for, configure, or trust features you do not need.

I originally published a more detailed version of this guide on the SSHFlow blog.

I'm also building SSHFlow — an SSH client where every server gets its own workspace for terminals, SFTP, code, and databases.

A useful distinction: SFTP support is not the same as a graphical SFTP file manager. OpenSSH provides command-line tools such as sftp; a client with a visual file browser is a better fit if you want to drag and drop files. Similarly, SSH port forwarding carries traffic through an SSH connection; it is not the same thing as an embedded remote-desktop client.

Match the alternative to your setup

You want a free desktop terminal

Tabby is a free, open-source terminal for Windows, macOS, and Linux. It offers SSH sessions, tabs, split panes, and customization through plugins. It is a reasonable choice if you want a configurable desktop workflow and do not need Termius-style synced hosts across desktop and mobile devices.

Tabby is based on Electron, and its maintainers do not describe it as lightweight. Choose it for its features and customization rather than assuming it will use fewer resources than another client.

You need SSH, graphical SFTP, and tunnels on Windows

Bitvise SSH Client is a free Windows option with SSH, a graphical SFTP interface, and port-forwarding features. The client is free for use in business environments too; its optional paid license concerns support and upgrade commitments. Bitvise SSH Server is separate software, so do not confuse the client’s terms with the server’s.

MobaXterm may fit if your Windows toolbox also needs RDP, VNC, or an X server for displaying remote Linux GUI applications. Its free Home edition has limits, so check the current edition terms before adopting it for a team or a larger set of sessions.

You mostly transfer files

WinSCP is designed around file transfers rather than being a full SSH terminal manager. It supports graphical transfers, scripting, and directory synchronization. If you mainly connect to upload releases or manage remote files, that focus may be an advantage. If you also need interactive terminal sessions, pair it with an SSH client or choose a tool that combines both workflows.

You want a minimal, command-line setup

Windows includes OpenSSH as an optional feature, and it is commonly available on Linux and macOS. You can connect directly from a terminal:
