title: LiteLLM Router — Stop Hardcoding One Provider Into Your App
summary:
Your support bot is fine until OpenAI returns 429s for twenty minutes.

If the app called openai.OpenAI() with a single model string, those twenty minutes are an outage. Not because the product broke — because you married one vendor in the client code.

LiteLLM gives you one OpenAI-compatible interface over 100+ providers, plus a Router that retries inside a model group and falls back to another group when the primary keeps failing. Your feature code keeps talking "chat completions." Reliability lives in the router config.

What you're solving

Most teams start with:

from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()
client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=...)

That is fine for a prototype. In production you eventually want:

  • A second provider when the first is rate-limited or down
  • The same message shape no matter which model answers
  • Retries that do not require rewriting every call site
  • A place to log cost and failures without sprinkling try/except everywhere

LiteLLM's answer is: keep the OpenAI client shape, move provider choice into a model_list + Router.

Install and make one call 

pip install litellm
# or: uv add litellm

SDK style (no proxy yet):

from litellm import completion
import os

os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"] = "..."
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "..."

# Same completion() shape for every provider
r = completion(
    model="openai/gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this ticket in one line."}],
)
print(r.choices[0].message.content)

r2 = completion(
    model="anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize this ticket in one line."}],
)

Every response is OpenAI-shaped. Exceptions map to OpenAI-style errors (RateLimitError, AuthenticationError, …), so existing handlers keep working.

Docs: Getting Started.

The workflow that matters: Router + fallbacks

This is the part you actually ship.

1. Define deployments under shared aliases

import os
from litellm import Router

model_list = [
    {
        "model_name": "support-summarizer",  # app-facing alias
        "litellm_params": {
            "model": "openai/gpt-4o-mini",
            "api_key": os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"],
        },
    },
    {
        "model_name": "support-summarizer-backup",
        "litellm_params": {
            "model": "anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5",
            "api_key": os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"],
        },
    },
]

2. Wire fallbacks and retries

router = Router(
    model_list=model_list,
    num_retries=2,
    fallbacks=[{"support-summarizer": ["support-summarizer-backup"]}],
)

Retries stay inside the same model_name group. Fallbacks leave that group for the next one in the list. That split is deliberate: don't burn your backup provider on a flaky single request if another deployment of the primary can still answer. See Fallbacks and Router load balancing.

3. Call it like OpenAI

response = router.completion(
    model="support-summarizer",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "One-line summary. No preamble."},
        {"role": "user", "content": ticket_body},
    ],
)
summary = response.choices[0].message.content

Your ticket pipeline never imports Anthropic. If OpenAI rate-limits after retries, LiteLLM moves to the backup alias.

4. Log what still fails

Catch litellm.RateLimitError / APIError after fallbacks exhaust. Those inputs become tomorrow's eval set and a signal to raise budgets or add another region.

Optional: run the proxy instead of embedding the Router

If more than one service needs the same failover rules, run the LiteLLM AI Gateway and point every OpenAI client at it:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    api_key="sk-your-virtual-key",
    base_url="http://localhost:4000",
)
client.chat.completions.create(
    model="support-summarizer",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "hello"}],
)

Config YAML holds model_list, fallbacks, budgets, and virtual keys. Apps stay dumb; the gateway owns reliability.

When not to bother

  • One hobby script, one key, one model — a plain SDK is enough.
  • You already have a mature internal gateway with the same features.
  • Latency budgets are so tight that an extra hop or cross-provider fallback is worse than a brief 429.

Everyone else who has been burned by a single-vendor outage: put the fallback config next to the model list, not inside twelve call sites.

Checklist

  1. Replace scattered provider SDKs with LiteLLM completion or an OpenAI client pointed at the proxy.
  2. Give production jobs an app-facing model_name, not a raw vendor id.
  3. Set num_retries for transient failures inside the group.
  4. Set fallbacks to a different provider (or region) for sustained failures.
  5. Log exhausted fallbacks; treat them as product incidents, not "weird LLM noise."

  • Router — load balancing, retries, cooldowns
  • GitHub: BerriAI/litellm

title: How to Manage ViciDial Lists: Deactivate, Reset & Delete Leads
summary:
How to Manage ViciDial Lists: Deactivate, Reset & Delete Leads

Remove, reset, or purge unwanted contacts from ViciDial lists without corrupting call logs or orphaning agent records.

List management in ViciDial requires direct database access combined with understanding how leads link to call logs, agent activity, and callbacks. Deactivating a lead preserves history; resetting a lead clears its attempt count and status; deleting a lead removes it entirely but risks breaking referential integrity if done carelessly. This guide shows the exact SQL, CLI commands, and web interface steps to manage each operation safely.

Tested on ViciDial 2.14 (SVN 3555+) and 2.13, Asterisk 16/18, MariaDB 10.5+, PHP 7.4+.

Prerequisites

  • SSH access to the ViciDial server or a machine with remote MySQL client installed.
  • MySQL or MariaDB command-line client (mysql) or a GUI tool like DBeaver or phpMyAdmin.
  • Database credentials with SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE on the asterisk database.
  • Understanding of ViciDial list IDs (numeric identifiers for campaigns/lists).
  • A backup of the asterisk database taken within the last 24 hours.
  • Agent or admin access to the web interface at /vicidial/admin.php.

Deactivation (DEAD status) is the safest choice in production because it preserves call logs and agent accountability while removing leads from the dialing queue. Resetting clears the attempt counter and status, re-queuing a lead without losing history. Deleting is permanent and risks breaking callbacks and orphaning logs.

Always back up the database before bulk operations. Use START TRANSACTION and ROLLBACK if a query affects more rows than expected. After any bulk change, verify counts with SELECT queries and test with a single agent before resuming full-scale dialing. Run orphan log cleanup (DELETE from vicidial_log WHERE lead_id NOT IN...) monthly if you delete leads regularly, and add database indexes if bulk updates time out on large lists (100k+ leads).

Next steps: review the dialer campaign settings to confirm max-attempt rules are aligned with your deactivation policy, set up a monthly backup cron job if you have not already, and test a reset on a single lead during a quiet period to verify behavior matches your expectations.
